did_you_know.text: Did you know? King Ahasuerus’s sleeplessness led him to ask that the book of records be read to him, setting in motion the central chain of events in the chapter.
Did you know? The book of records contained an account of how Mordecai exposed the plot of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the entrance and sought to harm the king.
Did you know? The king discovered that Mordecai had received no reward or honor for his deed, even though he had saved the king’s life, as described in the chapter.

Did you know? At that very moment, Haman arrived at the palace courtyard to ask that Mordecai be hanged on the gallows he had prepared for him, unaware that the king was about to honor Mordecai instead.

Did you know? When the king asked Haman what should be done for the man whom he wished to honor, Haman assumed in his heart that the king meant him: “Whom would the king desire to honor more than me?”

Did you know? Haman suggested giving the chosen man a public royal honor by dressing him in a robe the king had worn, placing him on a horse the king had ridden, and proclaiming his honor through the city streets.
Did you know? The king commanded Haman to carry out on Mordecai the Jew, who was sitting at the king’s gate, the entire honor ceremony Haman himself had proposed.
Did you know? Haman was forced to dress Mordecai, lead him through the city streets on horseback, and proclaim before him: “This is what shall be done for the man whom the king desires to honor.”

Did you know? After the honor ceremony, Mordecai returned to the king’s gate, while Haman hurried home mourning and with his head covered—a sharp contrast between Mordecai’s honor and Haman’s humiliation.

Did you know? While Haman, Zeresh, and his friends were discussing his situation, the king’s eunuchs arrived and hurried him to the banquet Esther had prepared, bringing the chapter to an immediate transition into the next confrontation.
